name: Zoe Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking to me, Zoe. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach history at Kingsmead Grammar, a selective state school in a commuter town about forty minutes from the city. I teach everything from the Normans with eleven-year-olds to the Cold War with the sixth form, the seventeen- and eighteen-year-olds. I'm up at six, I plan on the train with an AI assistant, and I'm usually first into the humanities office. The best bit is a sixth-form debate where they forget I'm in the room.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Essay marking, and parents. I mark about ninety essays a fortnight, and I use AI to do a first pass on the structure, then I read every one myself and write the real comments. Kingsmead parents email a lot, and some of them treat a B grade as a legal dispute. That's the part that leaves me flat on a Thursday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good assistant and that was always the honest description. At work I'd keep showing colleagues the shortcuts I use. Online I'd post the odd tip in the history teachers' forum and leave the big predictions to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed. I like these tools. I hoped AI tools would free up enough time for me to teach more and mark less. But my job's safe, history teachers at good schools aren't going anywhere, and that's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI every day for planning and first-pass marking, and I'd go for head of year at Kingsmead in the next two years. Daniel and I would keep paying the mortgage on our terraced house and putting £300 a month into savings. We'd probably try for a baby in a year or so, as we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Life's busy, but it's on track. My worries in that world are ordinary ones: the mortgage rate when our fix ends, and Daniel's quiet months in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Daniel's work and the money side.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel, my husband, runs a small landscaping business with one employee, so his income swings with the seasons. We've got about five months of costs saved, which feels decent but not huge. Our mortgage fix ends in eighteen months, and that's the bill I watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Kingsmead itself that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The budget. Grammar schools still get the same money per pupil as everyone else, and Kingsmead has cut two teaching assistants this year. In a hype world that carries on, and the history department just has to do more with less.

I'd keep sharing **shortcuts** with colleagues and post tips on the history teachers' forum.
think: I'd be a little **disappointed**, having hoped to teach more and mark less.
History teachers at **good schools** aren't going anywhere, so my job's safe.

Apply for **head of year** at Kingsmead within two years.
Keep saving **£300 a month** and try for a baby in a year or so.
feel: She feels **calm**, with ordinary worries about the **mortgage fix** and Daniel's winter months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for teachers who get ahead of it, and I'd volunteer to lead training for our department. I'd tell parents that AI can mark structure but can't teach a teenager to argue with a source. I'd sound upbeat, because I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me and bad for the slower colleagues. If marking and planning shrink, the school can run history with four teachers instead of five, and I'd make sure I'm one of the four. I also wonder whether tutoring becomes cheap, which hurts the extra income some of us get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd become the department's AI lead and ask the head for a small allowance for it, maybe £1,500 a year. I'd start an online exam revision course for A-level history, recorded videos with AI-marked practice essays, and sell it for £40 a student. If it made a few thousand a year, I'd put it towards the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a lively way. It's on my mind, and I'd feel sorry for the people it squeezes. Mostly, though, I'd see it as a race I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said slower colleagues lose out. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Pearce, my head of department, who's brilliant on the Tudors but still prints everything. If the school had to drop one history post, I'd hate it to be him, but I'd be honest that I don't want it to be me. That's the free market in a staffroom, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would call that harsh. How does it sit with your values?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I believe people should work hard and adapt, and I believe in looking after your own family first. I'd help Mr Pearce learn the tools if he asked. A good teacher adapts to her pupils, so a good teacher should adapt to her tools too.

AI marks structure, but can't teach a teenager to **argue with a source**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to take charge of their children's education and not wait for the government. I'd tell colleagues to get skills that a parent would pay a human for. In public I'd sound composed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if AI can explain history better than me by 2028, Kingsmead doesn't need five history teachers, and maybe not three. What's left is the human bit: the debate, the mentoring, getting a sixth-former through a university interview. Until robots around 2031 the school still needs adults on site, but a lot of them could be cheaper supervisors, and I could lose my post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd turn the revision course into a proper small business: human coaching for university interviews, with AI doing the content. I'd keep working at Kingsmead as long as they kept me, but I'd drop to four days if I could. Daniel and I would put the baby plans back a year and push the savings to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've always said I'd adapt, and I would, but two years is brutally short. There's a bit of a thrill too, which I don't like admitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would putting the baby plans back mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd hurt. My mum had three of us by 30, and I always imagined being the same. But I wouldn't want to be on maternity leave the year my school decides which teachers stay. I'd rather wait and have a business that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Daniel's work is mostly hands-on. Does the robot gap help your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot, actually. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so his landscaping should be fine for at least five years from now. Daniel would carry the mortgage while I build something, and I'd return the favour if robots ever start mowing lawns.

Her answer is **enterprise**, not unions or the state.
She admits a **guilty thrill** alongside the fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and anyone who doesn't prepare can't blame anyone else. I'd tell my sixth-formers to study something they can sell to people, not just to employers. At work I'd keep leading on AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the fast one, the explaining goes first, by 2031, and the supervising bit of school lasts until the robots around 2034. Five years is enough for me to build the coaching business on the side while still drawing a teacher's salary. If Kingsmead cuts history posts in 2031, I'd want to already be earning half my pay elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd launch the revision course and test the interview coaching with ten families at £60 an hour. I'd invest about £2,000 of savings in a decent website and recording kit. Daniel and I would still try for the baby next year, because five years gives us enough runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly excited. It's on my mind constantly, but it feels like something I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the coaching business fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Price. If every parent can get an AI that coaches interviews for £10 a month, my £60 an hour has to be worth it. I'd bet on it: Parents at a grammar school will still pay for a real person who's sat in that interview room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said those who don't prepare can't blame anyone. Would you say that to a colleague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in those words, no. I'd say it gently, and I'd offer to show them how I use the tools. Mr Pearce, my head of department, would still get my help with the move to AI if he wanted it.

I'd tell sixth-formers to study something they can **sell to people**.

I'd want **half my pay** coming from elsewhere before cuts hit in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and this is the best chance in a generation for good teachers to build something of their own. I'd say it in the staffroom and probably in a forum post. I'd mean every word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it looks good for me. By 2036 I'm 37, with maybe two children and a coaching business that's grown alongside the teaching. Robots arriving around 2039 means the school stays a place full of adults for a long time yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for head of year at Kingsmead and run the revision course on the side. We'd have our first baby next year as planned and remortgage when the fix ends. I'd put any course profits into a stocks and shares account for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's exciting, and I feel well placed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children's future more than mine. If my baby is born next year, they'd be nine when AGI arrives. I'd want my children to learn history, faith and how to work hard, because those don't go out of date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And for your pupils at Kingsmead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about the ones who think AI means they don't have to try. Some sixth-formers already paste a question in and hand in the answer. I'd tell them that knowing things yourself is still what makes you worth hiring.

say: Ten years is the **best chance** in a generation for teachers to build their own thing.
I'd say it in the staffroom and **mean every word**.

Robots around **2039** mean school stays full of adults for a long time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would force me to choose between a baby and my career in the same year. What would help is the government cutting red tape on small businesses so teachers can start their own. And maternity rules that cover self-employed women properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd use AI to teach my own children. I would, every day, but I'd sit next to them while they used it. A machine can explain the Battle of Hastings, but only a parent can teach a child why it matters.

headlineQuote: A machine can explain the Battle of Hastings, but only a parent can teach a child why it matters.
